title: Annie Laurie
description: The Scottish love song to Lady John Scott's tune, for 2 to 4 singers: two verses, slow and tender. The soprano sings the melody, which dips to middle C, the alto sings under it, joining it on the low notes and stepping above it at the cadences, the tenor fills in the chord and the bass sings the low line.

credits.words: an older Scottish song, said to be by Douglas of Fingland, reworked by Lady John Scott (1810-1900), who altered its second verse

licence.words: public domain: the older song, said to be by Douglas of Fingland, is printed in C. K. Sharpe's A Ballad Book (reprinted Edinburgh: Blackwood, 1880, pp. 107-108, archive.org/details/balladbook00shar, leaves n148 and n149); Lady John Scott, who altered its second verse (Moffat, The Minstrelsy of Scotland, p. 109, footnote), died 1900
licence.tune: public domain: Lady John Scott's (died 1900), who told Moffat the air was hers; the earliest copy in the British Museum is marked 1847 (Moffat, p. 109, footnote)
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella; its chords checked against the Hall printing's unsigned piano part and Finlay Dun's piano arrangement (Dun died 1853)
licence.source: melody and words from Annie Laurie (New York: William Hall & Son, 239 Broadway, plate 793; dated about 1848 by the Washington University catalogue, though the cover's Jenny Lind series points to 1850 or later; the cover, a portrait of Jenny Lind, lists it as No. 7 of eight songs), pp. 2 to 4, for voice and piano, with no composer, poet or arranger named, in C in 2/4 with each verse written out, and written here in C in 2/4 as printed; read from the scans at archive.org/details/b10258073 (page 2 at leaf n1, page 3 at n2, page 4 at n4); verses 1 and 2; checked against the same song "as sung by Catherine Hayes" (Cincinnati: W. C. Peters & Sons, and St. Louis: Balmer & Weber, plate 1484, dated about 1853), a new engraving of the same notes, archive.org/details/b10258115 (leaves n2 and n3), and against Finlay Dun's arrangement (St. Louis: Balmer & Weber, cover dated 1877, plate 692), archive.org/details/b10013751 (leaves n1 and n2), and Alfred Moffat, The Minstrelsy of Scotland (London: Augener, preface to the second edition 1896, this printing 1920), p. 109, archive.org/details/minstrelsyofscot00moff (leaf n128), which print the same tune; in verse 2 "throat is like the" fills a sixteenth more than the bar in the Hall printing (a dotted D); written here as Peters prints it, "like" an E sixteenth slurred to a D quaver; the grace notes before "dew" and "swan" left out; the four piano bars between the verses left out; Hall prints "And its", Peters "And it's", written "it's"; breaths written in for beginners: "true," before "Which", "be;", "rie," before "I'd" and "dee." before verse 2 (verse 1), and "swan;", both "on," and "e'e" (verse 2) shortened; the last "dee." held through the closing rest
